q: The 1966 White Paper is credited with starting modern EMS mainly because it documented:
why: The White Paper showed high trauma deaths, and that push started modern EMS.

q: An Emergency Medical Technician (EMT) gives care under whose license?
why: You and the paramedic work under the medical director's license; that doctor is legally responsible.

q: Offline medical direction is best described as:
choices: standing orders you follow without a phone call
radio orders you request for that one call
a refusal form you leave at the scene
a hospital report you write after transfer
why: Offline direction is standing orders, so you treat without calling.

q: On a dangerous scene, who is first in the safety order?
why: You first: you cannot help if you become a patient.

q: You park about how far from a fire, crash, or hazmat scene?
why: Park 100 feet from fires, crashes, and hazmat.

q: Alcohol-based hand sanitizer is OK on clean hands if it is at least:
why: Sanitizer needs at least 60% alcohol if hands are not dirty.

q: Causation in a negligence claim means:
choices: your breach produced the patient's harm
you owed the patient a legal duty
you broke the accepted standard of care
the patient suffered money damages only
why: Causation means the breach actually produced the harm.

q: You start care, then leave a patient who still needs it without an equal or higher handoff. That is:
why: Abandonment is leaving without consent and without equal or higher handoff while they still need care.

q: You find no pulse, no breathing, and fixed pupils, but you are not sure they are dead. You:
choices: start CPR after a living will
why: Presumptive signs are not enough. If there is doubt, start CPR.

q: During a radio report you should:
why: Keep the radio plain, and do not say the patient's name.

q: You catch a written error on a patient care report (PCR). You:
choices: erase the words and correct it
draw one line and correct it
cover the words and correct it
scrap the page and rewrite it
why: Draw one line through the error and write the correct words. Never erase.

q: When you start a patient interview, you should ask:
why: Open-ended first, then closed yes-or-no if you need to pin details down.

q: Two rescuers are doing infant CPR. You compress with:
why: Two rescuers on an infant use two-thumb encircling. Alone, the test default is the heel of one hand.

q: Semi-Fowler position is a sitting angle of about:
why: Semi-Fowler is 30–45 degrees; Fowler is 45–90.

q: Chest pain. Your partner is an EMT. You:
why: Request paramedics. Your partner is an EMT.

q: A patient is breathing 16 times a minute with good chest rise, looks short of breath, and saturation is 88%. You give oxygen with:
choices: a bag-valve mask at 1 breath every 6 seconds
why: Adequate breathing plus distress or sat under 94% gets a non-rebreather at 10–15 L/min, not a cannula.

q: An adult is not breathing but still has a pulse. You ventilate with:
choices: a bag-valve mask, 1 breath every 2–3 seconds
a bag-valve mask, 1 breath every 10 seconds
a bag-valve mask, 1 breath every 30 seconds
a bag-valve mask, 1 breath every 6 seconds
why: Inadequate breathing or apnea gets a bag-valve mask. Adult rate is 1 breath every 6 seconds.

q: For chest pain you think is a heart attack, the aspirin dose is:
why: Give 160–325 mg chewed (2–4 baby tablets of 81 mg = 162–324 mg).

q: Do not take a wheeled stretcher (gurney):
why: A gurney is not for stairs, off-road ground, or angled slopes that can tip.

q: For shock with no other position rule, place the patient:
why: Shock is supine and flat now. Do not raise the legs.

q: A pregnant patient past 20 weeks is transported:
why: Left lateral offloads the uterus from the aorta and vena cava (supine hypotensive syndrome).

q: A patient who fell from a ladder is sorted first by:
why: MOI is for trauma; nature of illness is for medical calls.

q: If you skip body substance isolation (BSI) or scene safety:
why: Skip BSI or scene safety and you failed.

q: An unstable or critical patient is reassessed every:
why: Unstable is every 5 minutes; stable is every 15.

q: The platinum 10 minutes is the goal for:
choices: time from injury to the operating room
scene time from wheels-stop to wheels-roll
time from the 911 call to your arrival
time from the hospital door to surgery
why: Platinum 10 is pull-up to start driving; the golden hour is injury to surgery.

q: The number-one airway obstruction in an unconscious patient is the:
why: When they go unconscious, muscles relax and the tongue falls back.

q: You suction a dirty airway until it is clear, for no more than:
why: Suction until clear, max 10 seconds, same for every age.

q: You insert an oropharyngeal airway (OPA) only if the patient is:
choices: unresponsive and has a gag reflex
alert, talking, and protecting the airway
why: OPA is for fully unresponsive with no gag. Gag on insert means pull it now.

q: Do not place a nasopharyngeal airway (NPA) if there is:
choices: a gag reflex with no trauma
why: Any head or face trauma is a hard stop for an NPA; a gag is actually a reason to use one.

q: Oral glucose is for low blood sugar if they:
choices: have a gag and cannot swallow
are seizing with a clenched jaw
why: One tube if sugar is under 80 and they can protect the airway; unconscious is a no.

q: Aspirin given for suspected heart-attack chest pain works by:
choices: keeping platelets from clumping so the clot does not grow
dissolving the clot already stuck inside the coronary artery
widening the coronary arteries the same way nitroglycerin does
blocking pain signals as they travel up the spinal cord
why: Aspirin makes platelets slippery so a clot does not grow. It does not dissolve clots.

q: Hold nitroglycerin if systolic blood pressure is under:
why: You need a triple-digit systolic (at least 100) before each nitro dose.

q: Shock means:
choices: high blood pressure in the brain
why: Shock is hypoperfusion: not enough oxygenated blood to cells, and waste piles up.

q: In compensated shock, blood pressure is often:
why: Early shock can still hold pressure. Do not wait for hypotension to call it shock.

q: When cells switch to anaerobic metabolism in shock, the main waste is:
why: Anaerobic work makes less energy and lactic acid, which feeds acidosis.

q: Cardiac tamponade is suggested by shock plus:
choices: quiet lung, tracheal shift, and chest wall pain
clear lungs, falling sat, and sudden dyspnea
fever, flushed skin, and a slow pulse
JVD, muffled tones, and narrowing pulse pressure
why: Beck's triad is narrowing pulse pressure, JVD, and muffled heart tones.

q: The first step when you pick up an automated external defibrillator (AED) is:
why: Turn the AED on first and follow the voice prompts.

q: Chest compression rate is:
why: Rate is 100–120 per minute, not just “at least 100.”

q: Adult compression depth is at least:
why: Adult depth is at least 2 inches, or 5 cm.

q: Stridor is:
choices: a high-pitched lower-airway sound at the mouth
a high-pitched upper-airway sound at the mouth
a low-pitched mucus rattle at the mouth
a bubbling alveolar crackle at the mouth
why: Stridor is a high-pitched upper-airway sound you can hear standing in front.

q: Fever, night sweats, and coughing blood is the classic picture of:
why: TB is fever, night sweats, and hemoptysis; you wear an N95.

q: On a short transport, a hypoxic chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) patient:
why: On short runs you still give oxygen. Do not withhold it for hypoxic drive.

q: An implanted cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) shocks from inside the chest. While it fires you:
choices: take your hands off the patient
unzip the vest on the patient
keep your hands on the patient
why: An ICD jolt is low and internal, so you can touch them when it fires.

q: A patient with a ventricular assist device (VAD) is talking but you cannot feel a pulse. You:
choices: start CPR for the missing pulse
why: Many VADs have no palpable pulse; if they are talking, they are perfusing.

q: A wearable external defibrillator vest warns that it will shock. You:
why: A vest is a wearable AED. Hands off while it shocks.

q: For an arm-drift check, the palms should face:
why: Arm drift is palms up, eyes closed, so you can see one arm drop.

q: Last known well is the last time the patient was:
why: Last known well is last seen normal, not when you arrived.

q: A patient looks like a stroke. Before you lock in that impression, first:
why: Low sugar can copy a stroke. Check sugar first, and do not give aspirin for stroke.

q: The appendix sits in the:
why: The appendix is at the start of the large intestine in the right lower quadrant.

q: You are the only rescuer doing infant CPR. You compress with:
why: Alone, the test default is the heel of one hand. Two rescuers use two-thumb encircling.
